children: Shoppers are looking for more discounts, but Deckers Outdoor doesn't plan on obliging.

Executives of the shoe company said consumers are becoming more cautious about how they spend their dollars, which led to slower sales of Hoka sneakers and Ugg shoes in the latest quarter. However, Deckers plans to keep selling shoes at full price, even though that choice is resulting in a lower revenue outlook for the year.

"I assure you we will compete aggressively, but we're not participating in the race to the bottom," Chief Executive Stefano Caroti told analysts Thursday. "Experience has taught all of us that the right approach in this environment is to continue to build your brand, to keep inventories tight and to really focus on full-price selling."
Shares declined 7% to $79 in after-hours trading.

Deckers said it now expects annual sales to be $5.7 billion to $5.73 billion, down from its earlier projection of $5.86 billion to $5.91 billion. The company lowered sales growth projections for both Hoka and Ugg.
The lower sales guidance came after revenue in the latest quarter rose 3.5% to $1.48 billion, missing analysts' forecast of $1.51 billion.

Sales of Hoka shoes rose 7% to $677.2 million, below analysts' projection of $690.6 million. Ugg sales were $786.4 million, also missing Wall Street's expectations of $800 million. Direct-to-consumer sales fell 1.8%, while wholesale revenue was up.
Net income was $313.1 million, or $2.31 a share, compared with $268.2 million, or $1.82 a share, a year earlier. Analysts were anticipating $1.79 a share.

The sneaker industry is suffering from excess inventory of casual lifestyle sneakers, which has prompted many shoe sellers such as Foot Locker and Nike to slap on discounts. Deckers' sales growth was slowing in the previous quarter, but investors were hopeful that the company's focus on popular performance running shoes would keep it afloat long-term.

More consumers are starting to wear performance sneakers including Hoka as casual daily-wear shoes, Deckers executives said Thursday. That trend is blurring the line between the performance and lifestyle categories, meaning promotions in one segment bleed over into the other, management said.

Deckers' strategy is to spend more on marketing and creating new shoe styles, rather than discounting its existing pairs. Leadership is hopeful that this will protect the company's reputation after gaining immense popularity over the past few years with Hoka.

"What we don't want to get into is a heavy promotional environment where you're seeing a lot of promotion across multiple franchises," Caroti said. "We can maintain better health just by staying clean with a bigger focus on that lifestyle."

Deckers did raise its earnings outlook, thanks to a boost from tariff refunds. It now anticipates earnings per share to be $7.80 to $7.95, up from $7.35 to $7.50. Tariff refunds net of tax are adding a benefit of 52 cents a share for the full-year.
